summary: The Gemara discusses the weight of the crimson thread used with the red heifer and the Yom Kippur goat, resolves a dispute about whether a non-priest may slaughter the red heifer, digresses on the customs of the people of Jericho, and concludes with the ish iti's impurity from carrying the Azazel goat.

display.whats: How much did the crimson thread weigh, and when does the ish iti become impure?
display.hint: Two disputes run in parallel: the weight of the crimson thread (for parah vs. Yom Kippur goat) and whether a non-priest may slaughter the parah. R. Yochanan boldly contradicts his own teacher on the latter.
display.title: Crimson Thread Weights and the Non-Priest Slaughter Dispute

learning.ahaMoment: R. Yochanan publicly contradicts his own teacher because he is convinced that non-priest slaughter is always valid - one of the few cases where a student overrules his teacher on record.
learning.memoryAnchor: Crimson thread: 10 zuz for the red cow, 2 sela for the Yom Kippur goat - and R. Yochanan tells a tanna to 'go teach that outside' when the tanna claims otherwise.
learning.learnerQuestion: How much did the crimson thread weigh for each rite, and may a non-priest validly slaughter the red heifer?
learning.coreTension: A baraita's crimson-thread weights for the red heifer and the Yom Kippur goat sit alongside a live dispute over whether the parah may be slaughtered by a non-priest, with R. Yochanan breaking from his own teacher's ruling that such slaughter is invalid.
learning.coreMove: R. Yochanan rejects the baraita's claim and the position of his own teacher R. Shimon ben Yehotzadak, ruling that non-priest slaughter of the parah has never been found invalid, while the digression on Jericho's customs and the ish iti's impurity round out the daf's practical details.

takeaway.text: The crimson thread weighed ten zuz for the red heifer and two sela for the Yom Kippur goat; R. Yochanan rules that non-priest slaughter of the parah is valid, even overruling his own teacher on the matter.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may conflate the non-priest slaughter dispute (about the parah) with the Yom Kippur goat rite, since both share the crimson-thread theme on this daf, when the slaughter debate is specifically about parah.

misconceptions.misconception: The dispute over whether a non-priest may slaughter applies to the Yom Kippur goat sacrifice, since both are discussed together with the crimson thread.
misconceptions.correction: The non-priest slaughter dispute is specifically about the parah adumah (red heifer); the Yom Kippur goat is a separate rite, linked on this daf only by the shared crimson-thread theme.

sugyot.finalRuling: The ish iti becomes impure by carrying the goat; he must immerse and wait until nightfall.

glossary.en: The designated man who escorts and sends the Azazel goat to the wilderness cliff on Yom Kippur.
Red heifer - a cow whose ashes purify those contaminated by a corpse.
One who has immersed in a mikveh but not yet waited until nightfall for full purification.

rashiTranslations.en: Of the heifer, the weight is ten zuz, since it requires heaviness. Of the goat, since it requires dividing,
the weight is two selas, and that suffices for it. Of the leper, since neither this consideration nor that one applies, it
suffices with a shekel. This is our reading: Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta and the Sages dispute regarding the heifer.
'And a sign' - so that you not err and say that one Sage held the weight to be two selas,
let this Mishnah serve you as a sign, for we learned in tractate Menachot
(110a): both the one who gives more and the one who gives less
fulfill their obligation, provided he directs his heart to Heaven; by this sign
you will remember to say that one Sage gave it the measure of
the one who gives more than all of them, and the other Sage gave it the measure of
the one who gives less than all of them, but a middling measure
was not mentioned here. 'They do not dispute regarding the heifer' -
only regarding the terminology used for the heifer. 'And that day' - when they disputed about it,
Ravya bar Kisi passed away; that is a Sage's name.
'Atones' - the death of the righteous atones,
as is stated elsewhere (Moed Katan 28a):
why was Aaron's death juxtaposed to the priestly
garments? To tell you: just as the priestly garments
atone, so too the death of the righteous atones.
'Of his bull' - the High Priest's bull of Yom Kippur.
'Elazar and a statute' - Elazar is written regarding it, 'and you shall give
it to Elazar the priest' etc. (Numbers 19),
and it is written there, 'this is the statute of the Torah,' and wherever
the word 'statute' is written, it is indispensable. 'Aaron and a statute' -
as it is written (Leviticus 16), 'and Aaron shall bring
the bull of the sin-offering that is his, and shall atone,' etc., 'and he shall slaughter
the bull of the sin-offering that is his,' etc. And it is written
in Acharei Mot on the same matter (ibid.), 'and this shall be
an eternal statute for you, to atone for the Children of Israel.'
'Slaughter is not a service' - and the statute does not
apply to slaughter. 'The heifer is different, for it is of the sanctity of
Temple upkeep' - that is, it does not have the sanctity of
the altar, but rather mere monetary sanctity,
since it is slaughtered on the Mount of Anointing; therefore
no aspect of divided services applies to it, and all
its services are equal. 'And is this not a fortiori
conclusion?' - as a rhetorical question: regarding the slaughter of his bull, which is of the sanctity of
the body, no statute is written, yet regarding the slaughter of
the heifer a statute is written and it is disqualified by a non-priest.
'Regarding the appearances of plagues' - as it is written (Leviticus 13),
'if it appears like a plague, he shall be brought to Aaron
the priest.' 'And he shall slaughter it before him' - from the fact that it is written
'before him,' it follows that the slaughtering does not pertain to Elazar
directly, but rather another person slaughters it before
Elazar. 'And Rav holds' - Elazar actually slaughtered it himself,
and 'before him' means that he should not divert his attention from guarding it.
'For only now does the heifer become fit' - since
its entire being is made only for its ash.
'To exclude what?' - that a diversion of
attention does not disqualify the performance of the heifer ritual. 'The gathering of its ash' - 'and a pure man shall gather,' etc.
(Numbers 19). 'And the filling of water' - to place into the ash for sprinkling. 'For sanctification' -
this is the placing of water on the ash and mixing them together.
